name: Rosa Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Rosa, thanks for doing this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential. Is that okay with you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Totally fine. I'm actually curious what other people are saying, though I know you can't tell me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Fair enough. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a senior drill operator at an iron ore mine, and for the last year I've been the lead on the autonomous drill trial. So half my week I'm in the cab of a blast-hole drill, and the other half I'm in a portable office at the edge of the pit, supervising three drills that run themselves and stepping in when one gets confused by broken ground. I do the handover notes, flag faults to the vendor's engineers, and train whoever's next. I love the problem-solving. What wears me out is the fly-in, fly-out roster, two weeks on site and one week home, because my partner Mei is in the city and I miss her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest. I've seen what the drills can do, and I thought it would go further. But I'd also say, good, now we can make the tools we've got work properly for the people using them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It probably means I stay a top operator for a long time, which is fine. I'd get bored, though. I like being the person who knows the new thing, and if nothing new comes, I'm just good at the old thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the trial and push the company to use the drills to take people off the night shifts, not off the roster. I'd do a part-time engineering degree online, because I've wanted to for a while. Money's fine, I'd just keep investing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Where, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use one to sort my fault logs, so I can see patterns, like drill three always loses its position fix near the old haul road. I use it to write handover notes and to check my answers when I'm studying. And I use one for planning trips home, which is a lot of logistics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the trial stalls, what happens to your role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd go back to being a nice feature. They'd keep one drill on autonomy and I'd be back in a cab most shifts. I wouldn't mind for a year or two.

S0.say: She'd admit to being a bit disappointed, having seen what the autonomous drills can do. She'd also say it's a chance to make the existing tools work properly for the people using them.
S0.think: She expects to stay a top operator for a long time, but would get bored without new technology to master.
S0.do: Keeps leading the drill trial and pushes the company to use automation to cut night shifts rather than jobs. Starts a part-time online engineering degree and keeps investing.
S0.quote: I like being the person who knows the new thing, and if nothing new comes, I'm just good at the old thing.
S0.fieldNote: Rosa defines herself by being first to understand new systems, so a plateau leaves her restless rather than relieved. Her progressive streak shows in wanting automation to cut night shifts, not jobs. Her daily AI use is practical and specific, especially fault-pattern sorting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where the workers have to get organised, because it's all going to be decided in the next few years. Automation can be good for everyone if the savings get shared. I'd say that out loud, even in the crib room where people roll their eyes at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally it's good. I'm the person they'd want running the control room, and I'd be paid more. But I'd be watching friends get moved off the trucks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a formal role as automation supervisor, with pay to match, and get a certificate in robotics maintenance through the company. I'd sit on the union's technology committee to push for redeployment instead of redundancies. I'd also teach a weekly session for operators who want to learn the system, on paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for me, but guilty around the edges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some of your colleagues may lose seats while you gain. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not great. I'd be the one teaching the robot that replaces Gary, and Gary taught me to drive a haul truck. I'd want to know there's a job on the other side for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think the union should ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Redeployment first, then retraining on full pay, then a share of the productivity gains. Every tonne the robots move faster is money. Some of that should land in the people's pockets who made it possible.

S1.say: She'd say workers need to get organised now because this will all be decided in the next few years. Automation can benefit everyone if the savings are shared.
S1.think: Personally she sees it as good news: she'd likely run the control room and be paid more, but she'd watch friends lose their truck seats.
S1.do: Asks for a formal automation supervisor role and a robotics maintenance certificate through the company. Joins the union's technology committee to push for redeployment over redundancy, and runs a weekly training session for operators on paid time.
S1.feel: Calm about herself, guilty about colleagues.
S1.quote: I'd be the one teaching the robot that replaces Gary, and Gary taught me to drive a haul truck.
S1.fieldNote: Rosa is one of the few people who'd gain directly from this picture and she knows it. Her guilt is personal: the trainer who taught her to drive trucks is the one she'd help replace. She fuses adaptability with progressive demands, asking for a share of productivity gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for public ownership of some of it. If machines do all the work, then who owns the machines is the only question left. I'd say it online and I'd say it at the union, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means even my control room job is gone. The AI would watch the drills better than me. Being early doesn't help when everyone arrives at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sit down with my financial adviser and move my savings into something solid, probably a chunk into an index fund and the rest into cash. I'd join a campaign for a national dividend from automation, and I'd use my trial experience to help the union negotiate. I'd keep working right up until they switch me off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, because I've got money and time is the thing I'm short of, not cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're used to staying ahead. What happens to that here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My whole edge is being six months ahead of everyone else, and in this one six months is nothing. I'd have to find a new edge, and I don't know what it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mei?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to stop worrying about my roster. If this happens I'm coming home for good, one way or another. That's a weird silver lining.

S2.say: She'd say this is the moment for public ownership of some of the machines, because who owns them becomes the only question left.
S2.think: She thinks even her control room job goes, since AI would watch the drills better than her. Being early doesn't help when everyone arrives at once.
S2.do: Meets her financial adviser in the first month and moves savings into an index fund and cash. Joins a campaign for a national automation dividend, helps the union negotiate using her trial experience, and keeps working until she's switched off.
S2.feel: Anxious but not panicked, because money isn't her short supply, time is.
S2.quote: My whole edge is being six months ahead of everyone else, and in this one six months is nothing.
S2.fieldNote: Rosa's usual strategy of staying ahead stops working in two years, and she names that plainly. Her strong savings and lack of children keep her from alarm. She finds an unexpected upside in ending the long-distance roster with her partner, Mei.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get the rules right if we start now. I'd push for a robot levy, so mining companies pay into a fund for every worker the machines replace. I'd be posting about it and probably annoying people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to move up and over. I'd be the one helping companies install these systems for a few years. After that, who knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd finish the robotics certificate and apply for a commissioning job with the drill vendor, the people who set the robots up at new sites. I'd stay in the union and push for the levy. And I'd put more into investments, because owning a slice of the machines seems smart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a real threat, but I can see the path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two, I'm reacting. With five, I get to be the one who installs the robots, and then I can see the cliff coming from the top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you want to land by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the city with Mei, working for the vendor or a public agency that oversees automation. Something where I'm on the inside of how it's done.

S3.say: She'd say five years is enough to get the rules right, pushing for a robot levy so mining companies pay into a fund for each worker replaced.
S3.think: She thinks five years lets her move up and across into installing these systems for a few years, though she can't see past that.
S3.do: Finishes the robotics certificate and applies for a commissioning job with the drill vendor in the first year. Stays in the union pushing for the levy and puts more into investments.
S3.feel: Uneasy, seeing a real threat but also a path.
S3.quote: With five, I get to be the one who installs the robots, and then I can see the cliff coming from the top.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Rosa from reacting to positioning. She'd move to the vendor side, which brings her closer to Mei in the city. She openly holds a contradiction: campaigning for a levy while working for the company selling the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift, if we don't waste it. Use it to rebuild training, to set up the levy, and to make sure mining towns have something else going before the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be thirty-seven. I'd have had a full career in automation, probably moved to the city, maybe changed fields twice. It's still the end of paid work for most people, so I'd want my politics sorted before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd start the engineering degree part-time and keep running the trial. By year three I'd move to the vendor, by year six into something like regulation or policy. All along I'd be pushing the union and the government to plan it out together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly because the end of it feels so big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time in your field. What would you do with year one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year I'd do a lot of listening, honestly. I'd talk to the operators at the other sites who've done this already. I'd rather learn from the people who got burned than the people who sold the matches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a longer runway change your politics at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me more patient. I'd want to build things that last, like proper public funds, not just fight fires.

S4.say: She'd say a decade is a gift if it isn't wasted, and should be used to rebuild training, set up a levy and give mining towns something else before the robots arrive.
S4.think: She expects a full career in automation in the meantime, probably in the city, but still sees the end of paid work for most people and wants the politics settled first.
S4.do: Starts a part-time engineering degree in the first year while running the trial, aiming to move to the vendor by year three and into regulation by year six. Pushes the union and government to plan together.
S4.feel: Uneasy, because of how big the end point is.
S4.quote: I'd rather learn from the people who got burned than the people who sold the matches.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Rosa plans a whole career arc, from operator to vendor to regulator. Her progressive views get more patient rather than less urgent. She'd learn first from workers at sites that have already automated, not from the sellers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I can adapt fast, but not that fast, and nobody else can either. What would help is a public fund paid by the companies using the robots, and a vote on how it's spent, so it's not left to the companies.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether I think it's good. Maybe I'm odd, but part of me wants it. Nobody should have to breathe pit dust for twelve hours, so a robot doing it is fine by me if the money is shared.

headlineQuote: Nobody should have to breathe pit dust for twelve hours, so a robot doing it is fine by me if the money is shared.
portrait: Rosa Young is 27, a senior drill operator at an iron ore mine who leads the autonomous drill trial and works a fly-in, fly-out roster away from her partner Mei in the city. She uses AI tools every day for fault logs and handover notes, has strong savings and investments, and sees herself as the person who knows the new thing first. She is calm in the mild pictures, even gaining from Steady Disruption, and anxious only when AGI arrives in two years and her head start disappears. With five or ten years she would move into commissioning and then regulation while campaigning for a robot levy and public funds.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because she can adapt fast but not that fast, and nobody else can either.
whatWouldHelp: A public fund paid for by companies using robots, with a public vote on how it's spent.
